Go from the explanation to the source, with the right version in hand.

This book separates three kinds of material: protocol specifications, implementation documentation, and original teaching examples. An example name, diagram, or latency budget is illustrative unless explicitly identified otherwise.

The protocol baseline

The IETF baseline is Media over QUIC Transport, draft-21, published September 8, 2026. Chapters link to relevant sections of that pinned version. Consult the current document status for later revisions and the MoQ working group for the broader standards effort.

Read the object model before the wire-message tables. Once tracks and groups make sense, the fields become answers to recognizable problems rather than an arbitrary list of integers.

A route through the MOQT specification

Start with the question you are trying to answer. These links all refer to draft-21, so their terminology and section numbers belong to the same edition.

Question Where to read
What identifies a piece of content? Objects (§2.1) and track naming (§2.4.1)
How do groups and subgroups organize it? Subgroups (§2.2) and groups (§2.3)
How do I follow new content or request older objects? Subscriptions (§3.1), fetch (§3.2), and joining an ongoing track (§3.5)
How are publications discovered? Namespace discovery (§4)
Which work gets sent first, and when does it stop? Priorities (§5.1) and delivery timeouts (§5.2)
What happens when peers connect? Session establishment (§6.2), initialization (§6.3), and stream usage (§6.4)
What can a relay retain and forward? Caching relays (§7.1) and relay object handling (§7.7)

Read the explanatory sections first, then use control messages (§9) when you need field layouts. The words MUST, SHOULD, and MAY express requirement levels in specifications. In particular, a recommendation is not a guarantee that every implementation will behave identically.

The transport underneath

RFC 9000 defines QUIC’s transport, including streams, flow control, and cancellation. RFC 9001 describes its use of TLS. RFC 9002 covers loss detection and congestion control.

RFC 9221 defines the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. Read it when deciding whether a small payload should be retried or replaced, and when checking message-size constraints.

Choose a source by the question

You do not need to read every specification before experimenting. Use a tutorial to build a model, implementation documentation to operate software, and a pinned specification to settle a protocol detail.

You want to… Start here Keep in mind
Understand the transport promises TCP specification and QUIC overview TCP bytes, QUIC streams, and MoQ objects are different units
Start a local player moq.dev quick start Its implementation model is not identical to the pinned MOQT draft
Explain blocked audio MDN autoplay guide Browser policy can prevent playback after successful delivery
Inspect a QUIC trace visually qvis Your implementation must export a compatible trace
Resolve a request or stream rule Draft-21 stream usage Read the version used by your implementation

Browser interfaces

The W3C WebTransport specification describes the browser API for streams and datagrams. Its presence does not remove the need for a protocol library above it.

The W3C WebCodecs specification describes low-level codec interfaces. It is useful for understanding decoder configuration and frame ownership. It does not define a full media player.

The WebRTC comparison

The early comparison uses the W3C WebRTC specification for the browser interface. The network behavior comes from IETF documents: RFC 8835, section 3.4 covers connection establishment with ICE and relay support, while section 3.5 identifies the media and data transports.

For media, WebRTC uses SRTP, the secure form of the Real-time Transport Protocol. Data channels use SCTP, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol, carried inside DTLS, Datagram Transport Layer Security. You do not need to learn these packet formats to understand the comparison; the distinction is that WebRTC specifies how these pieces fit together for real-time communication.

RFC 7667, section 3.7 explains selective-forwarding media servers. It supports the important point that a WebRTC conference can distribute media through a server; it need not connect every participant directly to every other participant.

The moq.dev implementation

Start with moq.dev and the concepts guide. Then read the separate explanations of moq-lite, hang, and transport choices.

For experiments, use the setup and development documentation. For a reachable relay, read the production guide. These pages describe a particular project and can evolve independently of this book’s IETF baseline.

Editorial approach and limitations

The protocol baseline was reviewed on September 16, 2026; this editorial pass and the linked setup resources were checked on September 22, 2026. The guide emphasizes stable ideas and avoids presenting a moving wire format as permanent. Draft-sensitive explanations refer to draft-21; implementation-specific examples are labeled with the project name.

This guide does not claim measured performance results, exhaustive browser compatibility, or successful execution of the upstream walkthrough. The latency values are invented examples. Validate a chosen stack and revision in your own deployment before relying on particular behavior.

Keeping an edition accurate

When updating the book, record the new research date and protocol revision together. Review terminology, setup, subscription behavior, timeout semantics, and the media-format boundary before changing the edition badge.

Keep examples identified as examples. If you add benchmarks, publish the workload, hardware, network conditions, implementation versions, and measurement points. If you add runnable SDK code, pin dependencies and verify it against the corresponding relay. An explanation is most useful when readers can tell exactly what it establishes.
